parakeet: Let's ask the critical question that often gets overlooked. What does it really mean for a belief to be true? This isn't a question about emotions, it's a question about evidence. If a belief can't produce public, testable evidence, something anyone could verify or falsify, then it remains a private conviction, not a shared reality. Now that may sound harsh, but it isn't meant to tear down faith. It's meant to ensure we treat every worldview with intellectual integrity and honesty. Whether you believe in a resurrected carpenter, an Islamic prophet, a cycle of rebirth governed by karma, or no deity at all, you owe it to yourself to ask, how would I know beyond a doubt that this claim corresponds to something real? By defining truth as that which corresponds to objective reality, what philosophers call the correspondence theory, we refuse to let emotional resonance or centuries-old tradition masquerade as proof. Ultimately, this is not an exercise in cynicism, but in consistency. If you demand rigorous proof for a guru's resurrection in India, you must demand the same for Jesus. If you dismiss a Hindu miracle because it can't be tested, you ought to dismiss any unverified Christian or Islamic miracle as well. By holding every claim to one objective yardstick, we protect ourselves from confirmation bias and tribal favoritism. Only then can we begin an honest inquiry into what, if anything, truly maps belief onto reality. So what do we mean by true? True here isn't just a fancy synonym for what I feel in my heart or what my community has always believed. In both philosophy and science, truth is tied to that correspondence between our claims and the way things actually are, what philosophers call the correspondence theory of truth. In other words, a statement isn't true simply because someone believes it. It must accurately reflect something out in the world or beyond it, if the claim is metaphysical. A poem can move you deeply or a sermon can stir your emotions, but neither counts as objective proof of a metaphysical claim. When we say truth corresponds to reality, we mean that if Christianity makes a claim about, say, a historical resurrection, it ought to be anchored in evidence that others can investigate. Archaeological records, reliable eyewitness testimony, reproducible phenomena, or some other publicly examinable data. If I say water boils at 212 degrees Fahrenheit at sea level, anyone can test that. If I say God raised Jesus from the dead, what public testable benchmark do I point to? Without that, it remains a matter of personal conviction, not something that matches reality in an intersubjective sense. Philosophers like Carl Popper made falsifiability central.
